case_name: Pembroke Civic Hospital v. Ontario (Health Services Restructuring Commission)
text:
Re Pembroke Civic Hospital et al. and Health Services

Restructuring Commission; Pembroke General Hospital,

Intervenor

[Indexed as: Pembroke Civic Hospital v. Ontario (Health

Services Restructuring Commission)]

36 O.R. (3d) 41

[1997] O.J. No. 3142

No. 394/97

Ontario Court (General Division),

Divisional Court,

A. Campbell, Then and Matlow JJ.

July 25, 1997

*The Court of Appeal (McMurtry C.J.O, Robins and McKinlay

JJ.A.) dismissed the application for leave to appeal the decision

of the Divisional Court on September 10, 1997.  See [1997] O.J.

No. 3603 in the OJ database.

Hospitals -- Restructuring -- Judicial review -- Hospital restructuring -- Health Services Restructuring Commission -- Commission ordering closure of non-denominational hospital and restructuring of denominational hospital operated by Roman Catholic Church -- Commission entitled to consider tradition of denominational health care in Ontario -- Commission not exceeding jurisdiction nor failing to provide procedural fairness in making its decision --
Public Hospitals Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. P.40, ss. 6
,
9(10)
-- Ministry of Health Act,
R.S.O. 1990, c. M.26
-- O. Regs. 87/96, 88/96.
The Health Services Restructuring Commission ("HSRC") ordered the closing of the Pembroke Civic Hospital ("PCH") and the restructuring of the Pembroke General Hospital ("PGH"), a hospital operated by the Roman Catholic Church. The PCH sought judicial review of the HSRC's decision. It argued, amongst other things, that (a) the HSRC had exceeded its jurisdiction by considering policy matters relating to preserving denominational health care systems in Ontario; (b) there were procedural defects because the HSRC did not provide PCH with adequate disclosure of the case it was expected to meet and had refused to provide it with lists and copies of all the submissions made by others; and (c) the Commission's decision contravened the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
.
Held, the application should be dismissed.
The court's role is very limited in reviewing the decisions of the HSRC.
Sections 6
and
9(10)
of the
Public Hospitals Act
, together with O. Reg. 87/96 under the Public Hospitals Act and O. Reg. 88/96 under the Ministry of Health Act, give the HSRC enormous powers, without any right of appeal to the court, to close hospitals or order them to amalgamate and to make directions for the complete restructuring of all aspects, including governance, of hospital services throughout Ontario. The court has no power to inquire into the rights and wrongs of hospital restructuring laws or policies, the wisdom or folly of decisions to close hospitals or decisions to direct particular governance structures. The only role of the court is to decide whether the HSRC acted according to law in arriving at its decision.
Ontario has a long history and deep tradition of diversity in the governance of hospitals including their operation by denominational organizations such as the Roman Catholic Church, the Salvation Army, and the Seventh Day Adventists. The HSRC was entitled to consider this reality, and it did not exceed its jurisdiction by so doing.
There was no procedural unfairness. There was nothing improper in the HSRC's contacts with the Roman Catholic Health Association. It was the duty of the Commission to consult and it properly did so. The HSRC was a policy-making and implementation body, not an adversarial forum. It was not obliged to adopt the adversarial procedures of a court or to provide production and discovery. It was obliged to give the PCH a fair opportunity to make its views known to the commission before it issued directions and it did so. The language of the "case to meet" principle had great application to adversarial proceedings where there is a lis between two adversaries. It had much less application to a complex polycentric decision like that of the HSRC in restructuring the local health care system. In the immediate case, it was clear that PCH knew in more than general terms what case it had to meet in relation to the very issues about denominational governance that it was raising before the court.
The Charter challenge was premature and speculative since there was no complaint of a present infringement. On the ground of prematurity alone, the challenge should be dismissed. However, because of the attention devoted to this issue some review should be made of the
Charter
arguments about freedom of conscience and religion and about alleged violations of
ss. 7
and
15
of the Charter. These arguments focused on health care services involving sexuality, reproduction and abortion. The PCH's apprehension of religious influence on health care appeared to have been based on the by-laws, and mission, values, philosophy, and ethical statements of the PGH. Its apprehension, however, appeared to have little, if any, foundation on the evidence about the health care actually provided in the hospital. There was no evidence that the Roman Catholic religion was forced on patients or that there was any attempt to indoctrinate patients. The presence of a cross outside the hospital and of crucifixes inside did not engage a Charter violation and did not infringe any Charter religious rights. There was uncontradicted evidence that there was no interference in medical decisions about obstetric and gynaecological health care. The closure of PCH would not impact on the current access to abortion services and the effect of the closure on potential future availability was speculative. There was no evidentiary basis for the various Charter challenges.
APPLICATION for judicial review of a decision of the Health Services Restructuring Commission.

Mary Eberts and Lucy K. McSweeney, for applicants.
John B. Laskin and Linda M. Plumpton, for respondent.
Bryan Finlay, Q.C., and Thomas A. Cromwell, for intervenor,
Pembroke General Hospital.

The judgment of the court was delivered by

ARCHIE CAMPBELL J.: --

The Facts

The facts are set out in the factums.

Urgency

Because the emergency department of the hospital is scheduled
to close on July 31, 1997, it is necessary to release these
reasons now in this abbreviated form instead of delaying for
more lengthy and elaborate reasons.

The Role of the Court

Hospitals are vital community institutions. They attract
strong loyalties and the prospect of hospital closure engages
strong feelings within the community. These deeply held views
and convictions are reflected in the evidence in this case.

The complex process of restructuring the health care system
is difficult not only for the Health Services Restructuring
Commission but also for each community affected by its work.

The court's role is very limited in these cases. The court
has no power to inquire into the rights and wrongs of hospital
restructuring laws or policies, the wisdom or folly of
decisions to close particular hospitals, or decisions to direct
particular hospital governance structures. It is not for the
court to agree or disagree with the decision of the Commission.
The law provides no right of appeal from the Commission to the
court. The court has no power to review the merits of the
Commission's decisions. The only role of the court is to decide
whether the Commission acted according to law in arriving at
its decision.

The Issues

The legal issues asserted by the applicant are these:

-- Jurisdiction

-- Procedural fairness

-- Disclosure and production of submissions

-- Civic's knowledge of the "Case to Meet"

-- The alleged parallel process

-- Prejudgment

-- Bias

-- Wrongful Exercise of Discretion

-- Constitutional

-- Do the applicants have legal standing?

--  Do the Commission's directions infringe the applicants'

Charter

s. 2(a)
guarantee of freedom of conscience and
religion?

--  Do the Commission's directions infringe the applicants'

Charter

s. 7
right to life, liberty, and security of
the person?

--  Do the Commission's directions infringe the applicants'

Charter

s. 15
equality rights?

--  Are any infringements justified under
Charter

s. 1
?

Non-Issues

The applicant does not argue that the powers delegated to the
Commission are illegal, overbroad, unsupported by or
inconsistent with the statute.

Jurisdiction

The applicants argue that the Commission exceeded its
jurisdiction by considering policy matters having to do with
the preservation of the existing role of denominational health
care systems in Ontario.

Ontario has a long history and deep tradition of diversity in
the governance of its hospitals. Of the 209 public hospitals in
Ontario 32, including the Pembroke General, are owned and
operated by denominational organizations including the Roman
Catholic Church, 29, the Salvation Army, and the Seventh Day
Adventists. The Commission was entitled to consider that
reality.

The Legislative Assembly in the Ministry of Health Act,

R.S.O. 1990, c. M.26
, and the government in the Regulations,
gave the Health Services Restructuring Commission a very strong
mandate to restructure the Ontario hospital system. To that end
the Commission has in law the power to direct the closing or
amalgamation of any hospital when it considers it is in the
public interest to do so. The Commission is given the power to
make any other directions it considers to be in the public
interest.

In Connelly v. Ontario (Health Services Restructuring
Commission),
[1997] O.J. No. 129
(Steele J., Ont. Div. Ct.
January 21, 1997) an unsuccessful motion by a Roman Catholic
hospital to stop the Commission's restructuring of the Sudbury
hospitals, the court referred to the Commission's strong
statutory mandate in relation to hospital restructuring and
reorganization. See also the stay application in this case,
Pembroke Civic Hospital v. Ontario (Health Services
Restructuring Commission),
[1997] O.J. No. 2749 (Gen. Div.)
, per
MacPherson J., at para 15.

Sections 6
and
9(10)
of the
Public Hospitals Act, R.S.O.
1990, c. P.40
, together with O. Reg. 87/96 under the Public
Hospitals Act and O. Reg. 88/96 under the Ministry of Health
Act give the Commission enormous powers, without any right of
appeal to the court, to close hospitals or order them to
amalgamate and to make directions for the complete
restructuring of all aspects, including governance, of hospital
services in every community throughout Ontario.

Although the Commission must consider the public interest,
its powers are virtually unfettered. The Commission is the
surrogate of the Minister. Regulation 87/96 under the
Public
Hospitals Act
provides that the Commission, in relation to the
Minister's powers under
ss. 6
and
9(10)
to close hospitals and
issue directions to the hospital administrator, may issue
directions in the place of the Minister. The Commission stands
in the shoes of the Minister and exercises the Minister's
powers. On the spectrum between political decision-making and
judicial decision-making, the Commission is close to the
extreme political/legislative end of the spectrum: see,
generally, Knight v. Indian Head School Division No. 19,
1990 CanLII 138 (SCC)
, [1990]
1 S.C.R. 653, 69 D.L.R. (4th) 489, and Whitley v. United States
of America (1994),
1994 CanLII 498 (ON CA)
, 20 O.R. (3d) 794 at pp. 807-08, 119 D.L.R.
(4th) 693 (C.A.).

The Commission has a broad policy mandate in relation to the
restructuring of local health systems throughout Ontario. The
Commission is under a duty "[t]o consider local hospital
restructuring plans provided by the Ministry and such other
information relevant to the plans as it deems appropriate". The
decision to consider representations from the Roman Catholic
Health Association of Ontario and to accept a role for Roman
Catholic Hospitals in Ontario generally, and Pembroke in
particular, is a policy decision in which the Commission and
its members, who are close to the political/legislative extreme
of the decisional spectrum, have the widest area of non-
reviewable discretion.

The Commission was entitled and required in the discharge of
its duty to consider the appropriate role in local health care
systems of denominational health care providers and it did not
exceed its jurisdiction by so doing.

Fairness: Disclosure and Production of Submissions

The Commission invited and received submissions from members
of the public and interested groups.

The applicant submits that there was a procedural defect
because the Commission did not provide the applicant with "the
case that [it] was expected to meet" and refused to provide the
applicant with lists and copies of all the submissions made by
others.

The Commission is a policy making and implementation body,
not an adversarial forum. As a policy making body, the
Commission is entitled to listen to anyone who may have helpful
information or opinions. Having invited and considered
submissions, it is under no obligation to follow the
adversarial procedure of discovery and disclosure of all the
information and materials submitted to it or considered by it.

The Commission was not obliged to adopt the adversarial
procedures of a court or to provide production and discovery.
It was obliged to give the applicant a fair opportunity to make
its views known to the Commission before it issued the
Directions, and it did so.

Fairness: Civic's Knowledge of the "Case to Meet"

The applicant submits that there was a procedural defect
because Civic was not given knowledge of the case it had to
meet within the meaning of cases such as Webb v. Ontario
Housing Corp. (1978),
1978 CanLII 1490 (ON CA)
, 22 O.R. (2d) 257, 93 D.L.R. (3d) 187
(C.A.), Nicholson v. Haldimand-Norfolk (Regional
Municipality) Commissioners of Police,
1978 CanLII 24 (SCC)
, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 311, 88
D.L.R. (3d) 671, Downing v. Graydon (1978),
1978 CanLII 1424 (ON CA)
, 21 O.R. (2d) 292,
92 D.L.R. (3d) 355 (C.A.) and Consolidated Bathurst Packaging
Ltd. v. I.W.A., Local 2-69,
1990 CanLII 132 (SCC)
, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 282, 68 D.L.R.
(4th) 524.

The language of "case to meet" has great application to
adversarial proceedings where there is a lis or issue joined
between two adversaries. It has much less application to a
complex polycentric decision-making task like the commission's
task of restructuring the local health care system in Pembroke.

It was obvious to everyone involved in the process that one
of the hospitals might be required to close and that the
spectre of Roman Catholic governance was a key issue. It had
been the subject of deep concern and great discussion in the
community ever since the publication of the Renfrew District
Health Council recommendations. It was no secret that one of
the options was to have one hospital with governance by the
Grey Sisters, the owners of the General, with a more
representative board. That option was explicitly set out with
the Commission's notice of intention to issue directions on
December 3, 1996 [v. II tab 10 p. 519]:

A second variant on the sole governance option would be to
allow current ownership of the General to prevail, and to
stipulate that the Hospital's governing board must be
representative of the community served. Based on the HSRC and
Minister of Health accepting a plan to be developed and
submitted by the Pembroke General Hospital, governance could
be structured so that the community is appropriately
represented on the board of the hospital. This would require
one administration, medical staff and medical advisory
committee, etc.

Under this option the Civic would be directed to close.

That option set out very clearly "the case that Civic had to
meet" to the extent there was a duty to do so.

The applicant submits that it was not enough for Civic to
know the "bare option" under consideration but that Civic was
in law entitled to know "what was on the Commission's mind when
it was thinking of the options". The applicant submits that the
Commission failed to disclose that it had under consideration
the concerns of the Roman Catholic Health Association and that
this represents a "new ground" of decision within the meaning
of Consolidated Bathurst.

It is obvious from the various submissions made by Civic that
it was very alive to the questions of denominational
governance, the appropriateness of denominational governance,
the Roman Catholic philosophy and mission of the General and
the question whether it is appropriate to have the General,
having regard to its denominational governance and philosophy,
to retain ownership of the single hospital in the community and
the service implications of that decision.

And in the face to face meeting between the Civic and the
Commission after the second round of written submissions there
was a very wide-ranging discussion of the Roman Catholic
governance issue.

It is clear that the Civic knew in more than general terms
what it had to meet in relation to denominational governance
and that it focused explicitly and directly on the very issues
it raises now in this court. It addressed on a number of
occasions the very things it now raises in this court,
particularly the compatibility of the Roman Catholic governance
of the General with the appropriate provision of all the health
services needed by the community.

Civic had a full opportunity to address the real issues at
stake. There was no mystery. Civic knew about and addressed the
very issues of Roman Catholic governance that it now addresses
in this court. There were no new grounds. Civic was not kept in
the dark about the essential issues. It knew, more than
generally, what it had to meet. It was given every opportunity,
and it exercised every opportunity, to meet what it had to
meet.

Fairness: Parallel Process

The applicant submits that in addition to the public
decision-making process there was a parallel undisclosed
process whereby the Commission secretly conferred with Roman
Catholic interests, particularly the Roman Catholic Health
Association of Ontario, of which General is a member, and its
president, Ron Marr, who was also a General board member.

The Commission has a power and a duty to inform itself about
the public interest in the health care system and, to that end,
to consult any person or organization and receive any
information which the Commission thinks can provide relevant
information or points of view.

The Roman Catholic Health Association had made general
submissions to the Commission and had contact with it about the
overall role of Roman Catholic health providers in Ontario.
There is nothing improper in that contact or those submissions.
It was the duty of the Commission to consult in that manner and
it did so.

The Roman Catholic Health Association made no submission to
the Commission about health services in Pembroke until January
1997 when it, along with the General and the Civic and many
others, including the Ontario Hospital Association and the
Nurses Association and the City of Pembroke and others made
submissions in relation to the December notices.

There was nothing improper about, and no procedural defect
in, the consultation and contact between the Commission and the
Roman Catholic Health Association of Ontario.

Fairness: Prejudgment

The allegation of prejudgment depends largely on the
examination of various staff discussion drafts and/or
recommendations and summaries of various points of view.

The existence of staff discussion documents setting out
particular points of view and policy options does not signify a
closed mind on the part of the Commission.

The Commission obviously did address and consider the
question of governance and the concerns of those who opposed
Roman Catholic governance.

The report of February 25, 1997, particularly at pp. 4-6,
demonstrates that the Commission was acutely alive to the
governance issue and the kind of concerns expressed by the
Civic about the Roman Catholic governance structure of the
General above the board level.

The Commission rejected the General's governance proposal,
and imposed a requirement that the new Board of Trustees must
be representative of the communities served and must reflect
the demographic, cultural, linguistic, geographic, ethnic,
religious and social characteristics of Pembroke and Renfrew
county and embrace a fair and equitable process of nomination
and election of community members to the Board of Trustees.

This does not demonstrate a closed mind. It demonstrates an
open mind.

Bias

The applicant's argument on bias is particularly thin. It
depends on the argument that the Commission had a closed mind
and that according to its executive director it did not "engage
in an analysis of these bylaws", which were a central part of
Civic's argument.

The Commission in its final report stated that it had
considered the submissions including the Civic submission that
referred to the bylaws. Apart from the 11-word answer of the
executive director, "No, we did not engage in an analysis of
these bylaws" that would be the end of this argument.

The import of this answer is open to different
interpretations. The applicant says it means the Commission
ignored the bylaws and the respondent says that it means that
the Commission did not need to conduct an independent analysis
of the bylaws because they were summarized and analyzed in
Civic's submission.

Whatever one takes from the answer, it provides no evidence
of closed mind or bias. The bylaws were one aspect of the
religious governance issue which was front and centre in
everyone's mind. The Commission and all the participants in the
process including Civic were clearly alive to the issue of
Roman Catholic governance, of which the bylaws formed part of
the detailed substratum. It was up to the Commission to
determine what weight it put on any aspect of any submission
and it was not obliged to engage in the exercise of parsing the
bylaws.

There is, on the basis alleged by the applicant, no evidence
of bias.

Wrongful Exercise of Discretion

There was no consideration of matters which ought not to have
been considered. The material from the Roman Catholic Health
Association was a proper matter to consider.

It is clear that the Commission did, as required, consider
the District Health Council Report.

Charter Prematurity, Indirectness and Standing

The Charter challenge is premature and speculative. There is
no complaint of any actual
Charter
infringement at this time.
The applicant's case is premised on the speculation that there
will be a Charter infringement in the future. The time to
challenge a Charter infringement is generally when there is an
infringement, not when there is mere speculation that a Charter
infringement may arise in the future.

On the ground of prematurity alone, the
Charter
motions
should be dismissed.

It is also doubtful whether Civic, a corporation, or Ms.
Lowe, who has not established that she has a need for any
health services in issue, have legal standing to assert a

Charter
challenge to the process.

Because of the attention devoted to them in argument,
however, some brief review should be made of the legal and
evidentiary basis of the
Charter
arguments.

General Freedom of Conscience and Religion

The Commission, at least implicitly, is obviously of the view
that it is in the public overall interest of the Ontario health
care system that there should be a role for Roman Catholic
hospitals such as the General. That is a policy question
squarely within the jurisdiction of the Commission.

It is the uncontradicted evidence of Jean Shifman, who is
Jewish, Debora and Mark Robbins, who are Pentecostal, Susan
Delarge, a Baptist, and Sandra Pitzner, a Lutheran, that there
was no religious influence in the health care they and their
families received at the General.

The applicants' apprehension of religious influence on health
care appears to be based on the bylaws, and mission, values,
philosophy and ethical statements of the General. Their
apprehension, however, appears to have little if any foundation
in the evidence about the health care actually provided in the
hospital. The evidence of Dr. Sharma, referred to below, is
particularly helpful on this issue. There is no evidence that
the Roman Catholic religion is forced on patients or that there
is any attempt to indoctrinate patients. There is no evidence
that the religious motivation of the hospital or its caregivers
constrains the chosen religious practices of any patient or
coerces their participation in any Roman Catholic religious
practice.

However religious may be the Corporation and its constating
documents it is the Board of Directors that runs the hospital.
The Board, under the directions of the Commission and the
facilitator, must be representative of the cultural,
linguistic, religious and socio-economic makeup of the
community served by the restructured hospital.

The applicants take issue with the fact that there is a cross
on the outside of the General and there are a number of
crucifixes in this Roman Catholic Hospital. The silent presence
of a hospital crucifix does not engage a
Charter
violation any
more than a Sikh turban worn by an RCMP officer.

The silent presence of crosses and crucifixes does not
constrain the chosen religious practices of those exposed to
them and does not compel or coerce them to engage in religious
practices or observances which they would not freely choose.

The silent presence of crosses and crucifixes in the Pembroke
General Hospital does not infringe any
Charter
religious
rights.

Equality Rights

To the extent this argument was separately addressed by
counsel for the applicants, it is only necessary to say that
the applicants have not established that members of any
disadvantaged groups will be disproportionally or even
adversely disadvantaged by any action of the Commission.

Evidentiary Basis of the Charter Challenges

The Charter ss. 7 and 15 challenges focus largely on the
availability of health services involving sexuality and
reproduction, particularly abortion.

The General performs vasectomies and tubal ligations but not
abortions. As noted below, neither the General nor the Civic
have performed an abortion in the past 14 years and perhaps
longer.

It is the uncontradicted evidence of Dr. Sharma, the Chief of
the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, that he has never
experienced any interference of a religious nature in carrying
out his medical responsibilities, including the insertion of
IUDs, the provision of birth control advice and prescriptions
for birth control pills, tubal ligations, and abortion
counselling. Dr. Sharma stated that he is unaware of the
content of the Roman Catholic mission statement and the related
institutional philosophies objected to by the applicants.

The applicant's submission on this evidence is as follows:

The fact that the Head of a Medical Department is so unaware
of the Hospital's core mission and values may indicate that
the Hospital is a place of great tolerance. However, for it
to be so lax about its essential values rather suggests that
the Hospital's and Commission's rationale for according it
pre-eminence in Pembroke could be a sham: if it is so
lackadaisical about its core mission and values, then there
is no reason for that mission to be taken into account in
policy making. In the alternative, one could regard Dr.
Sharma's evidence as simply anomalous and take no account of
it.

In argument, counsel for the applicant suggested that Dr.
Sharma was not candid. There is no basis in the evidence for
any such allegation. Nothing in the applicant's submission
detracts from the force of Dr. Sharma's uncontradicted
evidence.

For at least the past 14 years, no abortions have been
performed at any hospital in Renfrew county. Although one of
the applicant's deponents swore that there is a policy at the
Civic which precludes abortions, it appears that there are no
abortions anywhere in Pembroke because there is no doctor who
is willing to perform abortions having regard to the personal
risk of harassment or worse. Patients who require abortions are
now forced to go to other centres such as Almonte, Ottawa, or
Montreal. That situation, that lack of access to abortion
services, has obtained for many years and it has nothing to do
with the Commission or the closure of the Civic. It appears
that the post-merger availability of abortions to Pembroke will
be the same as the pre-merger availability and that it will be
similar to the situation in many parts of Ontario, where only
48 per cent of the non-denominational hospitals perform
abortions.

The closure of the Civic will have no impact on the current
access of Pembroke residents to abortion services. The effect
of the closure on potential future availability is speculative.

It is not necessary to pursue in detail all the other
allegations in relation to the provision of health care
services at the General, such as the availability of the
"morning after" pill, the disconnection of ventilators, the
ability of the laudable HIV/AIDS support group to continue its
work, and a number of concerns around reproductive health
issues. It is enough to say that these allegations are
generally unsubstantiated.

The applicants, to succeed, must prove that the adverse
effects which they allege will in fact occur or at least that
there is a high degree of probability that they will occur in
future. As noted above, Dr. Sharma's evidence is
uncontradicted. The evidence does not disclose a high degree of
probability that any
Charter
right will be infringed by the
General as a result of the health care environment contemplated
by the Commission's directions. The impact of the restructuring
on the current availability of health services appears on this
evidence to be essentially neutral.

There is therefore no evidentiary basis for the
Charter

challenges based on access to health services.

The other aspect of freedom of religion is the combined
effect of the directions of the Commission and the facilitator
that candidates for elected membership on the new Board (but
not the ex officio members such as the president of the
Alexandra club) would be required to sign a document agreeing
to respect the mission, values and goals of the hospital; treat
all employees in a fair and equitable manner; recognize the
contributions of the existing boards of the General and Civic
hospitals as an important function in developing a governance
structure.

Although one of the applicant's witnesses deposes that she
would not feel welcome on the new Board, there is no evidence
that the requirement of respect for the hospital's values poses
a good faith religious hurdle to anyone who might be interested
in joining the board.

There is a significant difference between a requirement to
respect the hospital's values and a requirement to support
those values or commit to them or agree with them or adhere to
them.

Having regard to the fierce nature of the public debate around
abortion, it may not be easy to require any participants in that
debate to respect the opposite point of view.

However difficult it may be to achieve mutual respect between
different points of view the public policy of Ontario, as
embodied in human rights legislation, requires an effort on the
part of every citizen to strive at least for mutual respect,
even when mutual agreement is not yet possible.

To require, as a condition precedent for a position on the
board of a public hospital, a public affirmation of respect for
the values of that hospital, without requiring adherence or
support or commitment or agreement with those values, does not
infringe any
Charter
right.

Conclusion

For these reasons, the application is dismissed.

Application dismissed.
